---
#title: "Coupled Framework"
---

## Dynamically coupled bio-hydro-morphodynamic modelling framework

To predict mangrove responses under different sea-level rise (SLR) scenarios, we developed a dynamically coupled bio-hydro-morphodynamic model that integrates the open-source hydro-morphodynamic model Delft3D Flexible Mesh (DFM) [@Kernkamp2011] with the Nature Based Solutions Dynamics (NBSDynamics) model [@Deltares2022]. This coupled framework enables the simulation of feedbacks between hydrodynamic processes, sediment dynamics, and mangrove vegetation development, allowing assessment of whether mangrove ecosystems can adapt to future changes in relative sea level.

As illustrated in @fig-coupling-framework, DFM resolves the physical processes governing coastal evolution, including hydrodynamics, sediment transport, and morphodynamic change. At each hydrodynamic time step, DFM calculates spatially distributed variables including water levels, flow velocities, inundation characteristics, and bed shear stress. These physical conditions are transferred to NBSDynamics, where they determine the suitability of local conditions for mangrove establishment, growth, and persistence. In particular, hydroperiod and bed shear stress represent key environmental controls on mangrove dynamics by influencing seedling establishment, vegetation stress, and the ability of mangroves to occupy and expand within the intertidal zone.

![Schematic representation of the dynamically coupled bio-hydro-morphodynamic modelling framework linking Delft3D Flexible Mesh (DFM) and NBSDynamics. The hydro-morphodynamic model provides environmental conditions that regulate vegetation dynamics, while updated vegetation properties modify flow resistance and bed roughness within the hydrodynamic model.](images/Coupling_framework.png){#fig-coupling-framework}

The vegetation model subsequently updates the spatial distribution and characteristics of mangrove vegetation based on the simulated environmental conditions. These updated vegetation properties are then transferred back to DFM, where vegetation-induced effects on hydrodynamics are incorporated through modifications of flow resistance and bed roughness. This two-way coupling allows vegetation feedbacks to influence the physical system, enabling the model to represent the reciprocal interactions between mangrove development and coastal morphodynamics. The coupled framework therefore captures both the ecological response of mangroves to changing environmental conditions and the role of vegetation in modifying hydrodynamic energy and sediment dynamics.

The coupling between DFM and NBSDynamics operates at a defined coupling interval, during which hydrodynamic and morphodynamic variables are exchanged between the two models. At each coupling step, DFM-derived variables are aggregated and provided to the vegetation model, which updates vegetation states based on the prevailing environmental conditions. The resulting vegetation characteristics, including spatial distribution and vegetation-related hydraulic parameters, are subsequently translated into DFM-compatible input fields for the following hydro-morphodynamic simulation period. This iterative exchange enables continuous feedback between vegetation development and coastal evolution throughout the simulation period.

Although mangrove ecosystems have the capacity to increase bed elevation through belowground biomass production and organic matter accumulation, which can enhance their ability to maintain elevation relative to rising sea levels, this adaptive mechanism depends on the balance between sediment dynamics, biomass production, and the rate of SLR. By explicitly coupling vegetation growth with hydrodynamic and morphodynamic processes, the modelling framework allows the potential for mangrove soil elevation gain and ecosystem persistence under different SLR scenarios to be evaluated.

The coupling interface was developed using Python and facilitates communication between DFM and NBSDynamics by exchanging model variables during runtime. Through this approach, the model represents the full feedback pathway between physical forcing and ecological response, including the influence of changing inundation conditions, hydrodynamic stress, vegetation development, and vegetation-induced modifications to coastal processes.
